3012.d:
String Theory is a rendering of long strands of information. A range is chosen, and a periodic function oscillates between these two values, its time based on the distance from the centre, snapped to values in the x/y diagonal.

Features:
3012.c:
Rotation: One of two values, equally likely. The image will either be in the x=y or x=-y axis.

Scale: This affects the spacing of the information strands. All values are equally likely.

Range: This affects the tightness of the waves within each strand, and allows patterns to form across adjacent strands.

Hue Range: Some values allow for changing hues within strands, others limit the hues to a specific, curated palette. These are of varying probabilities and will affect rarity.

3056.d:
"Debris, World" is the result of an algorithm that started in April 2021. It was called "Debris.js".
Spring was blooming all around the house, taking over the debris and remnants of ancient battles that stood here. Inspiration was everywhere.
The initial goal was to use mathematical formulas for creating patterns inspired by the density of nature, that could be used by a pen plotter, so it kept focusing on outputting vector lines. This history and practice produced a graphical style based on line strokes, plus occasionally some transparent, filled shapes.
Each artwork will be either Debris or World, for they are variations of two existing pieces from my workshop.
Each generative image allows for downloading a SVG file of the line art, ready for plotters -> just press 's' key in live mode when the computing has completed.
The "Format" feature tells you what machine size and paper size you would need, if you were willing to give it a try. A warning though, some of the SVGs can be tricky, servo-killers.
<3

3067.d:
Vortice Umbra: A companion piece to Vortice Lux.

Concentric ellipses rotate over time, producing phasing patterns. The ellipses are rendered with drop-shadows, with the direction varying over time. This produces emergent patterns light and dark interplay. Vortice Umbra features a dark background.

Features:

Spacing: A wider spacing produces bolder patterns and emphasis on the light and dark. All integer sizes from sixteen to forty-eight are equally likely.

Eccentricity: This affects the shape of the ellipses. An eccentricity close to one produces a subtle effect, whilst lower eccentricities of 0.9 emphasise the changes in the spiral.

- Train generative AI model in live NFT
- Show how AI learns along time & how it is evocative/puzzling
- Your AI is also a generator so what about a big shared gallery? ;)

Process
1- It generates 9 random shapes (no link, unique rarities)
2- You launch training & model learns to imitate images (1st artifacts ~1min, texts can take >10min)
4- You watch it learn (or forget) forever in evocative realtime mosaic of random samples

Controls
- H: hide/show help
- DblClick - Space: start/pause training
- Q/A-D: less/more tiles in mosaic
- S-W/Z: slower/faster tile refresh
- I: hide/show stats panels (Click to switch)
- X: save trained models (for future XPs)

More details on https://github.com/naibdian/naibdian-collections/blob/main/pixel.ai/README.md

The infinite origami has become unfolded. Directly beneath you, woven of crests and valleys, never repeated on this unending plane, lies this pattern in paper.

Written in vanilla JS & HTML5 Canvas.

Licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
3177.c:
A plane is repeatedly folded over itself, choosing creases either at random, or according to some pattern (like a grid). These creases form the boundaries of the individual textured tiles.

Once the folds are complete, they are undone in reverse order, recreating the original plane. With each unfolding, the orientation of each crease (as a mountain or a valley), and each tile (facing up or down) is recorded as a sequence of 1s and 0s. Tiles are colored and textured according to similarities in these binary sequences, giving rise to subtle symmetries and repetitions.

Written in vanilla JS & HTML5 Canvas.

An homage to my favorite abstract expressionist, Franz Kline. I never really "got" Kline, if I'm being honest, but one day about ten years ago, I walked in the MoCA in Los Angeles, and right inside the front door was Kline's "Butress," and it stopped me dead in my tracks. 3223.d:
"And so he spent his final years in solitude, watching the shadows move from dawn to dusk, seeing the lights of the city blink at night."


After launching "City Lights", I started animating some of the scenes to send as a gift to collectors. A few more iterations later, this started to feel like it deserved its own fxhash project, which turned into "City Life". This work attempts to evoke a meditative feeling by carefully balancing features like density, size and color. It aims to add a sense of depth with the most basic shading and perspective, and it suggests the presence of life merely through the play of light and shade. On a sufficiently powerful machine, each animation loop should take about a minute to complete. Press space bar in the live view to download an mp4 encoded video of the animation. London, December 2021.

3238.d:
Mountains, rendered as graphics layers, masked by six possible textured image layers, placed on a canvas. Each texture is generated fresh; there are no image files used. These textures are created in varying shades of gray, and shadows and some posterization added for further texture.

Features include… 

Population: Sparse, few, some, many. Basically, the number of mountains.
Width: Narrow, Thin, Medium, Wide. This is the width of the mountain base. All of them narrow to a point.
Height: Diminutive, Standard, Tall, Towering. Some mountain ranges are higher than others.

The extreme values of each feature are rarer, so a sparse population of thin, tall mountains, for example, is rarer.

3240.d:
A river meandering over a noise-based landscape. A line is drawn either horizontally, vertically, or more rarely, a ring. Time progresses for 1,000 iterations as the line travels, bends, and splits. 

There is a lot of variation on the line quality - from thin and controlled, to chunky and chaotic. It's a lot of fun to watch it run and see where it ends up.

I've been experimenting with this algorithm for a long time and this is the most visually interesting variation so far.
